title: Contact Surgery
notes: Open by naming the lecture's organizing metaphor: surgery is controlled replacement, not a decorative cut. The chapter starts with topological cut-and-paste, upgrades the cobordism to a Liouville handle, then spends real effort on the framing obstruction. The final third turns the construction into Legendrian surgery presentations and filling consequences.

title: The Surgery Move
notes: Begin with the purely smooth operation. The formula removes a framed tubular neighborhood of the attaching sphere and inserts the complementary product. The diagram should be read left to right: the attaching sphere determines the missing tube, and the replacement swaps which sphere is visible as the new belt sphere.

title: Cobordism As A Handle
notes: Translate the cut-and-paste into a movie. A handle cobordism has a lower boundary that remembers the old manifold and an upper boundary that is the surgered manifold. The core and cocore are bookkeeping devices: the core records what is attached, while the cocore records the belt sphere for the reverse move.

title: Why Contact Surgery Needs More Data
notes: Stress that a smooth handle is not yet a contact construction. Contact geometry needs a symplectic cobordism with a Liouville vector field pointing the right way near the boundary. The symplectization formula is the standard collar model, and contact surgery asks the handle to carry the same Liouville-flow logic.

title: Strict Neighborhood Input
notes: Use the neighborhood theorem as the local matching device. An isotropic submanifold is not determined only by its image; its symplectic normal bundle records the transverse contact-plane data. A strict contactomorphism of neighborhoods exists once the base diffeomorphism and the symplectic normal bundle isomorphism are aligned.

title: Weinstein Model Handle
notes: This is the analytic heart of the construction. The quadratic function g gives the handle its lower and upper levels, and the vector field Y is both Liouville for the standard symplectic form and gradient-like for g. The displayed one-form alpha zero is the contact form induced on the level hypersurfaces.

title: Contact Surgery Theorem
notes: State Theorem 6.2.5 as the first completed upgrade. If the isotropic attaching sphere has a trivialized conformal symplectic normal bundle, the model handle glues into a symplectic cobordism. The output contact structure is unchanged away from the surgery region, so the construction is local but its topology is global.

title: Natural Framing
notes: Explain why the word natural is doing work. A topological framing of an isotropic sphere splits into the Reeb line, the complex image of the tangent bundle, and the symplectic normal data. The first two are fixed by the stabilized tangent trivialization, so the chosen symplectic normal trivialization supplies the remaining freedom.

title: Framing Theorem 6.3.1
notes: Present the theorem as a compatibility test rather than as another construction. For dimensions with n greater than two, a framed smooth attaching sphere can be realized by contact surgery exactly when the induced almost complex structure extends over the handle. The dimension three Legendrian case needs separate care, which the next slides isolate.

title: H-Principle And Rotation
notes: The h-principle separates formal isotropic data from genuine isotropic embeddings. In dimension three, Legendrian regular homotopy of immersed circles is governed by rotation. The front formula is included because it makes rotation computable: downward and upward cusp counts record the winding of the tangent direction in the contact planes.

title: Stabilization Changes The Framing
notes: Use this slide as the warning for dimension three. Adding a zigzag always gives a negative twist relative to the contact framing and changes rotation by a sign. Positive twists are not freely available in tight contact manifolds because the Bennequin inequality restricts how large the classical invariants can become.

title: Contact Dehn Surgery Grid
notes: Now switch to the three-dimensional language. The contact longitude supplies the reference slope on the boundary torus, so the coefficient is read relative to the contact framing rather than a Seifert surface unless one is specified. The special coefficient minus one is the Weinstein handle surgery from Theorem 6.2.5.

title: The Plus-Minus One Warning
notes: Contact r-surgery is more delicate than topological Dehn surgery because the tight contact structure on the glued solid torus may not be unique. The coefficients one over k are better behaved, and plus or minus one surgeries become the natural algebra for presentations. The slide keeps that warning adjacent to the cancellation picture.

title: Cancellation Lemma
notes: Read the cancellation lemma as the local inverse law for Legendrian handle moves. A contact minus one surgery creates a belt sphere, and a contact plus one surgery on that belt sphere recovers the original contact manifold. The Liouville-flow picture is what identifies a Legendrian push-off with the belt sphere.

title: Ding-Geiges Presentation
notes: The presentation theorem is the payoff for the three-dimensional discussion. Lutz twists handle the passage to an overtwisted reference when needed, the Lickorish-Wallace theorem supplies an integer surgery description, and the contact conversion rewrites the result as plus or minus one Legendrian surgeries from the standard three-sphere.

title: Fillings And Tightness
notes: Close by showing why the surgery presentation matters beyond existence. It lets one cap strong fillings, attach handles after a weak filling is made locally strong near Legendrian knots, reduce to homology spheres, and finally prove that weak symplectic fillability rules out overtwisted discs. The dependency graph should make the tightness theorem feel engineered rather than mysterious.
